content.title: About
content.content: Maitake (Grifola frondosa) is an edible mushroom that grows in large clumps at the base of old oak and birch trees in temperate regions of Asia and North America. It has a delicate, slightly nutty flavor and a firm, meaty texture. Frequently used in traditional Asian cuisine and in health‑focused diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Japan, maitake is called the “dancing mushroom” and is revered as a longevity tonic.
The fruiting body can reach up to 30 cm in diameter and weigh as much as 1 kg.
Maitake contains beta‑glucans that are believed to boost immune function.
Commercial cultivation often uses sawdust blocks inoculated with mycelium.
Its dense texture makes it a popular meat substitute in vegetarian dishes.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Polysaccharides, especially beta‑glucans, stimulate macrophage activity and natural killer (NK) cells.

items.title: Blood‑sugar regulation
items.content: Studies suggest maitake extracts improve insulin sensitivity and reduce post‑prandial glucose spikes.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: The mushroom is rich in polyphenols and vitamin C, which help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Cardiovascular health
items.content: Beta‑glucans may help lower LDL cholesterol levels.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effects
items.content: Maitake extracts have been shown to decrease pro‑inflammatory cytokines.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to mushroom polysaccharides.

items.title: Blood‑pressure lowering
items.content: High doses can reduce blood pressure, which should be considered by people on antihypertensive medication.

items.title: Mycotoxin contamination
items.content: Improperly harvested or stored mushrooms may contain toxins; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Maitake can be sautéed, stewed, baked, or added to soups and stews. Before cooking, gently clean the mushroom, slice it, and briefly fry in oil. It pairs well with tofu, vegetables, or noodles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh maitake keeps in the refrigerator wrapped in a paper bag for 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight container for up to 6 months.
